cells.tense: You are giving from a full place, and it is landing where it is needed.
cells.act: choose which star to steer by and steer
cells.ask: Pick the heading your help takes this week — where it matters most — and follow that one. Other places can stay open until the next week.
cells.core:
Support is moving out of you and arriving. You know how to hold something up, and right now that's being used — a call answered, a weight taken off someone, a thing arranged before anyone had to ask. None of it is being calculated. It's operating.

What's less clear is the direction. Two or three places want the next portion of you, and from inside the fog they look equally plausible. You don't need to see the whole road. Pick the heading that matches what you actually want to have happen there, and follow that one for a week. The others stay open. They just don't get fed this week.
cells.sheetLine: Pick the heading your support takes, and hold it a week.
cells.verb: share your strength where it is actually needed
cells.place: in the fog where the next step is visible but the road is not

cells.tense: You are bracing already for the cost of helping before help has been asked.
cells.act: let the inner compass decide the small case
cells.ask: When a need seems to be forming nearby, hold still one breath and ask whether carrying it is actually yours. Let the small case decide, and move from what is on the table.
cells.core:
The reach out is real and it runs past the situation. You sense what a person will need before they've said it, and you're already moving — arranging, supplying, arriving early. From outside it reads as plenty. From inside, some scan hasn't fully powered down.

The difficulty isn't the helping. It's deciding from the picture you've assembled rather than from what's actually on the table now. Some of what you bring isn't needed yet, and carrying it costs you quietly. Before the next act of help, pause for a single breath. Let what's here answer the question instead of what you've already imagined. Then move, either way.
cells.sheetLine: You may be supplying the imagined need, not the one present.

cells.tense: You used to be the one people came to, and that door is behind you now.
cells.act: engage the hard part on purpose and see what holds
cells.ask: Stay inside a commitment that still has weight through the friction it brings — no sorting the whole life, just that engagement — and see what your strength holds.
cells.core:
Something has you holding back. Not hoarding — just not reaching. Help doesn't move out of you the way it once did, and offers that come your way don't get picked up. You're standing at a door you've already stepped past, and the fog doesn't help: when you can't tell what's solid, waiting becomes the whole posture.

You don't need the whole road to find out. Stay with a commitment that still has weight in it, even a small one, while it's difficult. That friction shows you what your strength is made of now. Waiting until you feel ready first would defeat the test; from here, readiness and engagement are the same move.
cells.sheetLine: Staying with a commitment through friction shows what still holds.
cells.verb: share your strength where it is actually needed
cells.place: in the fog where the next step is visible but the road is not

cells.tense: You are already steering the direction here, and calling it the circumstances.
cells.act: face one way for three days
cells.ask: For three days, choose a heading on purpose and hold it, even if it feels arbitrary and nobody sees. Notice how the week changes when the direction comes from you.
cells.core:
Look at what got arranged. Resources moved, people got covered, timing worked out. That wasn't the room doing it. Someone was steering — and it was you, though you've been telling it as what the situation required, as if the situation had preferences.

The blind spot is your own hand in where things have gone. For three days, pick a direction deliberately and keep to it, however small. You don't need a reason that would satisfy anyone. Notice what the week does when the heading came from you, instead of from whichever way things already leaned. The steering is what you're not seeing, not the outcome.
cells.sheetLine: You set this direction, and you've been calling it the situation.

attempts.check: The weakest claim is in Status 2, where I have the person auditing every hand they lend without support for the idea that this is disrupting their ability to read the room; the record says resources flow outward and here run past measure, which supports over-extension but not the exact interior scene of counting. A reader could reasonably say the audit isn't happening — they just give freely and get drained — and the ask (steer by what's actually needed, not by what you imagine is required) still works if that's the case, because either way the fix is looking at the actual situation instead of the imagined one. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you give too much,' which is a verdict rather than an observation; a person who does not experience their giving as excessive would bounce right off it.
